children: Nic Carter has a blunt message for the companies that turned their balance sheets into Bitcoin vaults. In his view, most of them aren't offering investors much they can't already get from a spot Bitcoin ETF.
Carter, a general partner at Castle Island Ventures, made the argument in an interview on October 27, 2026.

Bitcoin treasury firms, also called digital asset treasury (DAT) companies, are public companies that hold Bitcoin as a core part of their corporate strategy. The pitch to shareholders is that owning the stock gives you Bitcoin exposure plus something extra.
Carter's critique goes after that "something extra." He argues that for most of these firms, the extra is hard to find.

Spot Bitcoin ETFs are a cleaner route to Bitcoin exposure, one that skips the added risks that come with treasury companies. When you buy a treasury company's stock, you are also buying its management team, its capital decisions, its debt, and its corporate overhead. An ETF simply holds the asset and tracks it.
The market appears to have been reaching a similar conclusion on its own. Bitcoin treasury and DAT companies traded at discounts of approximately 40% to net asset value in early 2026.
A persistent discount suggests investors see the corporate wrapper as a cost rather than a benefit. That lines up neatly with Carter's argument that the wrapper often contributes little.

Carter isn't the only skeptic. Zac Prince, whom research findings connect to Galaxy Digital, has questioned the yield-generation strategies some treasury firms use to justify their premiums. His skepticism dates back to early 2026, and he has drawn parallels to past Bitcoin yield schemes.

The template for all of this is Michael Saylor's MicroStrategy, now known as Strategy and traded under the ticker MSTR. It is widely referenced as the original model for a public company holding Bitcoin as a treasury asset.
Strategy's approach inspired a wave of imitators. As of November 2026, the sector remains concentrated, with Strategy dominating thanks to the sheer size of its Bitcoin holdings.

Between 2025 and 2026, scrutiny of the sector intensified, focusing on NAV discounts and on whether these companies have sustainable business models that can actually outperform simply holding Bitcoin directly.

The arrival of spot Bitcoin ETFs sharpened that question considerably. Before ETFs, some investors bought treasury stocks because they were one of the few easy ways to get Bitcoin exposure in a regular brokerage account. Once ETFs filled that gap, the treasury firms lost a big part of their original appeal.

The sector has not been standing still. Treasury firms continue to experiment with capital structure innovations and new corporate strategies. Still, clear evidence of substantial operational value beyond capital preservation and Bitcoin exposure has been hard to find.

Because the sector is so concentrated, the largest players may be best positioned to argue that scale and track record justify their structure. Smaller copycats, holding modest Bitcoin stacks without a distinctive strategy, look most exposed to the ETF comparison.
Firms leaning on yield-generation to differentiate themselves now face skeptics like Prince, who see uncomfortable echoes of past schemes.

title: Nic Carter says most Bitcoin treasury firms offer little beyond ETF exposure
